editorial:
The Iron Mask (1929) is the capstone of Douglas Fairbanks's silent-era swashbuckler career â€” a sequel to his own Three Musketeers (1921), directed by Allan Dwan and released by United Artists on February 21, 1929. Technically a part-talkie, it carries a complete synchronized Vitaphone disc score and two brief spoken-word sequences in which Fairbanks addresses the audience directly as a departing D'Artagnan. The film copyright expired no later than 1985 under the 1909 Act's 56-year ceiling, and the source material â€” Dumas's Vicomte de Bragelonne (1847â€“1850) and The Three Musketeers (1844) â€” has been in the public domain for well over a century. A creator can adapt the story, the characters, and footage from confirmed original prints without clearing any underlying rights.

The rights trap is the score on most circulating copies. Kino Video's 1999 DVD restoration, produced with MoMA, dropped the original Vitaphone disc composition because those rights could not be cleared and substituted a newly commissioned orchestral score by Carl Davis. That score is a fully protected 1999 work independent of the film's public-domain status. Anyone pulling footage from the Kino disc and keeping the Davis music is using protected material without a license. The Internet Archive copy (identifier: TheIronMask) is a 72-minute truncation â€” substantially shorter than the 95-minute original â€” and its audio source should be verified before assuming it carries the free 1929 Vitaphone material.
faq: Can I use footage from The Iron Mask in my own film or video?

Yes for the footage itself â€” the 1929 film is definitively public domain in the US by term. The catch is audio: the Kino/MoMA DVD restoration carries a 1999 score by Carl Davis that is separately copyrighted. Use prints confirmed to carry the original 1929 Vitaphone score, or replace the audio entirely, to stay clear of that protection.
Is the Dumas source story free to adapt?

Completely. Alexandre Dumas's source novels â€” The Three Musketeers (1844) and Vicomte de Bragelonne (1847â€“1850) â€” are 19th-century works in the public domain worldwide. The characters, the Iron Mask plot, and all underlying story elements are freely adaptable without any licensing.
